Rust is a multi-paradigm language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1][2]. It draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Graydon Hoare started Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first released publicly in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2].

Rust does not use classes or inheritance. Instead, it builds behavior from structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this with runtime checks on array bounds and pointer dereferences [3], while C, C++, and Fortran allow unchecked pointer arithmetic [3].

{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a multi-paradigm language that prioritizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1][2]. It draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Graydon Hoare started Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. The language was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 following in 2015 [2].

Rust has no classes or inheritance. Instead, it builds behavior from structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java relies on runtime checks [3], whereas C, C++, and Fortran allow unchecked pointer arithmetic [3].

Rust's syntax resembles C++, yet it has no garbage collector [2]. Instead, it enforces ownership and borrowing rules at compile time, verifying memory access before the program runs.

Rust combines performance with memory safety, making it a strong choice for systems programming [1][2].

{"text":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a multi-paradigm language that prioritizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1][2]. It draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Graydon Hoare started Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. The language was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 following in 2015 [2].

Rust has no classes or inheritance. Instead, it builds behavior from structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java relies on runtime checks [3], whereas C, C++, and Fortran allow unchecked pointer arithmetic [3].

Rust's syntax resembles C++, yet it has no garbage collector [2]. Instead, it enforces ownership and borrowing rules at compile time, verifying memory access before the program runs.

Rust combines performance with memory safety, making it a strong choice for systems programming [1][2].","sources":"[1] Wikipedia: Rust (programming language)
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_%28programming_language%29
Summary: Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety. Rust supports multiple programming paradigms. It was influenced by ideas from functional programming, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching. Rust also provides structs, enums, traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional object-oriented programming, without relying on classes or inheritance.

[2] Wikipedia: Outline of the Rust programming language
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_the_Rust_programming_language
Summary: The following outline is provided as an overview of and topical guide to Rust: Rust is a multi-paradigm programming language emphasizing performance, memory safety, and concurrency. Rust was initially developed by Graydon Hoare starting in 2006, later sponsored and maintained by Mozilla Research starting in 2009, and first publicly released in 2010, with version 1.0 released in 2015. Rust is syntactically similar to C++ but guarantees memory safety without needing a garbage collector.

[3] Wikipedia: Memory safety
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety
Summary: Memory safety is the state of being protected from various software bugs and security vulnerabilities when dealing with memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers. For example, Java is memory-safe because its runtime error detection checks array bounds and pointer dereferences. By contrast, programming languages like C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic with pointers implemented as direct memory addresses with no provision for bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe.
